activities.anchor: the shop-with-unlocked-door hypothetical is the A-level classic
activities.caption: run the theories on the hard theft case
activities.name: aiTheftBranch

config.root: A theft that truly helps the needy at trivial cost to the owner. Run the three theories.

start.text: Kant's test first: can "take others' property when it suits me" be universalised?

choices.label: No — universalised theft abolishes the property institution the act relies on
choices.feedback: Theft fails the categorical imperative outright — the act destroys the practice it presupposes.

choices.label: Yes — one petty theft harms no one
choices.feedback: That is not Kant's test: universalisability, not the size of the harm, is what fails.

kant.text: Universalised, the maxim is rationally incoherent — so the verdict is unconditional, whatever the consequences for the needy.

util.text: Property rules create the incentives — investment, creation, exchange — whose collapse harms everyone; but the needy-helping, trivial-cost case is exactly the one the calculus finds difficult.

choices.label: And what does the act make of the agent?

virtue.text: A thief is practising dishonesty as a trait — the act is wrong for what it builds into character, whatever it produces.

config.why: Three theories, three fault lines: universalisability, incentive arithmetic, character.

activities.anchor: the proviso that every modern appropriation argument quietly reopens
activities.caption: fill the blanks — where property comes from
activities.name: aiPropertyCloze

config.text: Locke's labour theory: mixing %%0%% with unowned things creates title, provided "enough and as good" is left for others. The Statute of Anne (%%1%%) created authors' rights as an explicit bargain — %%2%%, not natural right — which is why each new copying technology relitigates the same utilitarian trade.
config.hint: What Locke said we mix; the year copyright was invented; the bargain's other half.

activities.anchor: the New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft over exactly this, December 2023
activities.caption: bet on where the scraping fight actually lives
activities.name: aiScrapePredict

config.q: Copyrighted works scraped to train large models: is the disagreement about the facts of copying, or about something else?
choices: The facts — what counts as a copy is objectively settled and the rest follows
The analogy — whether theft, learning or the library is morally load-bearing
config.why: The disagreement is not about facts: Kantians say the creator's consent is bypassed, utilitarians weigh incentive collapse against a genuine innovation externality — the analogies carry the argument.

activities.anchor: The research verdict is genuinely unsettled
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the games literature
activities.name: aiGamesSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary of the simulated-killing literature is wrong — click it:
lines: Plato wanted poets censored: representation trains the soul.
Aristotle replied with catharsis: drama purges emotion rather than exciting it.
The research verdict is settled: violent games cause real violence, and later studies only confirmed it.
Kant's test is brisk: "pretend to kill in a game" universalises harmlessly — no one is deprived of anything.
Desensitisation effects are measurable and modest; moral disengagement explains how players compartmentalise.
config.correction: It did not settle: the best-controlled large studies (Przybylski and Vuorre, 2020) find no relationship between game time and aggressive behaviour, and meta-analyses disagree about effect sizes.
config.why: The philosophically interesting residue is whether moral risk requires demonstrated harm or only plausible habituation — the old utilitarian-versus-virtue dispute wearing a controller.

activities.anchor: VR raises the stakes of the same question
activities.caption: drag the divider — the simulation frame cuts both ways
activities.name: aiVRCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — the simulation frame cuts both ways:

before.label: Immersion without a victim
before.text: VR raises the stakes of the corruption question: rehearsing cruelty at maximum immersion, with no one harmed — does habituation still work on character?

after.label: The inverted frame
after.text: If simulated worlds ever hosted real experiencers, the ethics of "just a game" would invert — a preview of the machine moral-status debate.

config.why: The same technology points outward at character and inward at moral status — the two debates share one frame.

activities.anchor: flagged high-risk at roughly twice the false-positive rate of white defendants
activities.caption: guess the magnitude — COMPAS error balance
activities.name: aiCompasEstimate

config.prompt: ProPublica's 2016 COMPAS investigation: Black defendants were flagged high-risk at about a 45% false-positive rate. Roughly what was the white false-positive rate?
config.why: About 23% versus about 45% — twice the rate — while the vendor's own metric was satisfied. Kleinberg's impossibility result is why "fair algorithm" is a policy choice wearing a formula.
